entry.dc:title: Estimation of mercury content in tailings of the gold mine area of Poconé, Mato Grosso, Brazil
entry.dc:creator: von Tümpling W.
entry.dc:description: As in many other parts of the world, gold is produced in the surface mining region of Poconé, Mato Grosso, Brazil, using mercury. The goal of this investigation was to estimate the amount of mercury in certain tailings and to determine the area of the land that has been contaminated by the gold mining operations. Mercury concentrations from 2 to 495 ng/g (dw) were determined in the tailing materials. It was observed that only isolated sites were acting as central points of contamination. Using digital Landsat satellite data (The-matic Mapper) and aerial photos, the sites degraded by the mining were classified, and their total area was estimated to be 12.3 km<sup>2</sup> in the region of Poconé. It was estimated, that 4.9 km<sup>2</sup> were occupied by the contaminated tailings. The mean height of the pile slags was determined to be 4.5 m. From the experimentally calculated average density of the material in the tailings, 2.01 g/cm<sup>3</sup>, the total mercury content in the piles of tailings was estimated to be 1600 ± 350 kg. © 1995, Ecomed Publishers. All rights reserved.

entry.dc:title: Tree survival and growth on land reclaimed in accord with Public Law 95- 87
entry.dc:creator: Chaney W.R.
entry.dc:description: The objective of this study was to determine survival and growth of black walnut (Juglans nigra L.) and northern red oak (Quercus alba L.) 12 yr after planting on a surface-mined site in southern Indiana reclaimed according to specifications of Public Law 95-87, the Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act of 1977. A stocking level adequate to meet the requirements for forest land use (1112 trees/ha, or 450 trees/acre) was attained only for black walnut and only if competing ground cover vegetation was controlled in the tree rows. Height of both tree species was significantly grater when ground cover vegetation was controlled during the first 2 yr, but the growth rate, approximately 10 cm/yr, was very slow.

entry.dc:title: Monitoring airborne dust from quarrying and surface mining operations
entry.dc:creator: Merefield J.R.
entry.prism:publicationName: Transactions Institution of Mining Metallurgy Section A
entry.dc:description: This note introduces the concept of "finger-printing' airborne dust samples on the basis of mineralogy by providing information on ambient dust levels before opencast mining and quarrying operations and a dynamic record during them. The intention is to provide site operators and regulators with the means to eliminate dust nuisance from disputes over planning and licence applications before it becomes a serious hazard. -Authors

entry.dc:title: Mining equipment into the 21st century
entry.dc:creator: Wiebmer J.
entry.dc:description: Several industry trends are putting new demands on surface mining equipment. This is true both on the 'hard' side of the equipment business - the research and product development programs, and on the 'soft' side - the business processes, human resources and competitive strategies. This article describes seven key industry trends and the impact each is having on surface mining equipment suppliers. These trends are, respectively, globalization, consolidation, improved asset management and utilization, a scarcity of skilled labor, environmental issues, cost competition, and information management.

entry.dc:title: Automating surface mines
entry.dc:creator: White J.W.
entry.dc:description: This is a truly exciting time in surface mining technology. A revolution is coming -- a revolution made possible by complete mine management systems working in concert with many devices currently available or in the prototype stage. By the turn of the century, the face of surface mining will indeed be different. Many 'futuristic' applications of advanced data processing to surface mining systems and individual mining functions are already available. Acceptance of such technology is beginning to take hold and will accelerate, despite some resistance in what is an essentially conservative industry. Examples of this new technology include drill monitoring, load weighing, equipment tracking systems, production reporting systems, and robotic haul trucks.

entry.dc:title: Possible use of wetlands in ecological restoration of surface mined lands
entry.dc:creator: Atkinson R.
entry.dc:description: Surface mining for coal has dramatically altered millions of hectares throughout the Appalachian region of eastern North America. Flat benches and vertical high walls have replaced well-drained slopes, and wetlands have developed 'accidentally' on abandoned benches. Surface mining is continuing in this region, but new regulations do not include specifications for wetland construction in the reclamation process. Recent research has suggested that many ecosystem services appropriate for the Appalachian landscape could be performed by constructed wetlands. Inclusion of wetland construction in a reclamation plan could lead to a net increase in wetland acreage locally, as well as offset the loss of natural and/or accidental wetlands. By studying accidentally-formed wetlands, we hope to determine what species can be established in wetlands that are constructed to enhance nontreatment goals in reclamation. Study sites included 14 emergent wetlands in Wise County, Virginia. Sampling in June and August detected a total of 94 species in 36 vascular plant families. Obligate wetlands species, species that occur in wetlands over 99 percent of the time, were found in all 14 sites and included 26 species. The presence of so many wetland species without intentional management efforts suggests that wetland establishment could become a common component of mine reclamation. © 1994 Kluwer Academic Publishers.

entry.dc:title: Evaluation of procedures to estimate biomass on surface coal mine lands reclaimed under the Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act of 1977
entry.dc:creator: Brenner F.J.
entry.dc:description: Current surface mine regulations as ascribed under the Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act of 1977 require that mine lands be returned to the approximate original contours (AOC) with an area coverage of at least 70% and to biological productivity equal to or greater than that which existed prior to mining. Six different procedures were evaluated on nine mine sites in northwestern Pennsylvania as to their suitability to estimate aboveground biomass on mines reclaimed as hayland and pastures. Biomass estimates determined by different procedures were compared to those obtained by random clip plots and with landowner estimates of the annual yield from each site. Biomass estimates determined from a disk meter and landowner interviews varied approximately ±10% from those obtained from random clip plots compared to a variation of ±8%-37% for the other procedures. The number of samples required to obtain reliable estimates within ±10% of the mean at 95% confidence intervals varied among the different sampling procedures according to the variance in biomass on the site. Although all procedures may be used either singly or in combination to estimate above ground biomass on reclaimed mine lands, the combination of the disk meter, profile board, and vegetation height is recommended because of their ease of measurement compared to the other procedures. © 1994 Springer-Verlag New York Inc.

entry.dc:title: Particle size distribution of an aerosol and its sub-fractions
entry.dc:creator: Verma D.K.
entry.dc:description: Particle size distribution of an aerosol and its sub-fractions was carried out as part of an epidemiological study by using a Retsch Precision High Volume Cascade Impactor.The impactor was used in the underground and surface mining operations as they are currently practised. It was also used in experimental stopes in gold, uranium and nickel mines where conditions of dry drilling were simulated. The impactor fractionates airborne dust into seven ranges of particle size from submicron to 32 μm aerodynamic diameter, when operating at 40 l. min<sup>-1</sup> Since the impactor operated at high flow rate, sufficient dust was collected to permit further analysis of the sub- fractions, such as free crystalline silica or metal (iron).A unique system was designed by using a venturi and compressed air for its use in an underground environment. For some tasks the particle size distribution of the sub-fraction was found to be similar to that of the total dust but different for other tasks. © 1994 British Occupational Hygiene Society.

entry.dc:title: Regulating in Space and Time: The Case of Regulatory Federalism
entry.dc:creator: Hedge D.M.
entry.dc:description: We outline and test an empirical model of federal regulatory behavior that reflects the spatial (i.e., interstate) and temporal dimensions of regulation within a federal system. A pooled time-series design is used to examine the interplay of national and subnational influences on the oversight decisions of officials at the U.S. Office of Surface Mining (OSM, Department of the Interior) during the period 1985–1989. The analysis indicates that the regulatory decisions of federal authorities at OSM reflect shifts in the nation's political climate, the freelancing efforts of individual members of Congress, and the states' political climates. Taken together, the findings suggest that national policymakers are able to direct the oversight activities of bureaucratic subordinates but are constrained in that regard by “botrrm iin”. © 1994, Southern Political Science Association. All rights reserved.

entry.dc:title: Automated downtime recording and processing for continuous surface mining systems
entry.dc:creator: Agioutantis Z.
entry.prism:publicationName: International Journal of Surface Mining Reclamation and Environment
entry.dc:description: A number of open pit mines, employing mainly continuous mining methods, are currently in operation at the lignite basin of Ptolemais-Amydeon in northern Greece. This study presents the design characteristics and implementation of a software system developed for a network environment, using a popular database framework, in order to facilitate recording and processing of downtime as well as generation of various equipment status and statistical reports for any period within a calendar year for chained production systems involving BWEs, conveyors and stackers. © 1994, Taylor & Francis Group, LLC. All rights reserved.

entry.dc:title: Continous surface mining equipment: how to achieve success
entry.dc:creator: Delilla E.
entry.dc:description: Continuous mining systems (bucketwheel excavators or continuous mining machines by Wirtgen, Voest-Alpine, etc.) must be matched to specific operating conditions. There are no "off-the-shelf' machines, and there are usually no simple modifications that will make a machine perform differently in response to changing mining conditions. In some cases, it has taken years for a mismatched machine to be made to perform effectively. There have been numerous cases where the machines were just not compatible with the conditions and never performed to expectations. Continuous mining systems can work. They offer an opportunity for high productivity at low operating costs for mining operations. However, everyone involved must be aware of the many tasks that must be successfully completed to apply these systems in their mines. -Author

entry.dc:title: Surface mining
entry.dc:creator: Dunn A.
entry.dc:description: This report gives an overview of worldwide surface mining operations during 1993. It emphasises the importance of regulations and adverse public opinion that severely restrict mining activity and gives examples of rehabilitation schemes. Coverage includes developments in and examples of highwall mining, drilling, fragmentation, crushing and breaking, continuous extraction and information technology. Developments and projection of future trends in machinery are covered. These include specific reference to hydraulic excavators, front-end loaders, rope excavators, dump trucks and continuous transport systems. -S.E.Long

entry.dc:title: Surface mining of Canadian coal
entry.dc:creator: Singhal R.
entry.dc:description: Canada's coal production is approximately 65.4 million tonnes of which 95% is produced by surface mining methods, mostly from the three Western provinces. The mines are highly mechanised; productivity gains during the past few years have ranged from 60-80%. This paper provides an overview of the Canadian coal mining industry vis-a-vis surface mining. -from Authors

entry.dc:title: Morphological characteristics of reconstructed prime farmland soils in western Pennsylvania
entry.dc:creator: Bell J.C.
entry.dc:description: The major soil horizons of prime farmlands disturbed by surface mining in the USA must be reconstructed during reclamation in accordance with current federal legislation. Consequently, the topsoil (Ap horizon) and subsoil (B and C horizons) are removed and stockpiled separately during overburden removal activities and are replaced over spoil during reclamation in an attempt to reconstruct the original soil profile and to help maintain soil productivity. This study was conducted to investigate the morphological, physical, and chemical properties of reconstructed mine soils and to identify characteristics of these soils that could limit crop growth. We described and sampled a total of 72, 1- to 2-year-old, reconstructed soil profiles at eight reclaimed surface mines throughout western Pennsylvania. Soil depth over spoil was generally >75 cm with an observed range of 5 cm to >2 m. Well- expressed Ap horizons were observed in nearly all profiles. The structure of the reconstructed subsoils was drastically altered by mining to a structureless and massive condition. Excessively compacted shallow soil layers restricted downward penetration of plant roots within 47% of the soil profiles described. Reconstructed soil horizons that are likely to restrict plant growth included horizons composed of spoil, horizons with >50% rock fragments and excessively compacted soil layers. These restrictive soil horizons were found within 1 m of the surface for 57 of the 72 soil profiles described and within 50 cm for 51% of the soil profiles. Morphological investigations of reconstructed soils could be useful for evaluating reclamation success and soil productivity potential.

entry.dc:title: Environmental planning in regulation and management of instream gravel mining in California
entry.dc:creator: Mathias Kondolf G.
entry.dc:description: In California, the mining of sand and gravel from rivers and streams is presently regulated under the state's Surface Mining and Reclamation Act of 1975 (SMARA), with 113 different countries and cities designated as lead agencies for approving reclamation plans and issuing special use permits. These agencies rarely have the technical expertise or resouces to assess cumulative impacts of instream mining or to monitor the sometimes subtle and frequently delayed off-site environmental impacts. Moreover, the concept of 'reclamation' is unsuitable for instream mining whose effects propagate upstream and downstream during mining and cannot be reversed by subsequent on-site reclamation. Instream operators also fall under the jurisdiction of other agencies, such as the US Army Corps of Engineers and the California Department of Fish and Game, but these agencies lack resources and a consistent approach to evaluate and mitigate the environmental effects of instream mining. Instream gravel mining can be properly addressed only by comprehensive environmental planning that evaluates all potential aggregate sources, including upland deposits, and the environmental impacts of their extraction. Aggregate extraction from rivers must be managed on the scale of river basins, while the demand for aggregate and the various sources of its supply must be managed on the scale of production-consumption regions. © 1994.
entry.authkeywords: Aggregate extraction | Gravel mining | River management | Wetlands

entry.dc:title: Radiation exposure at the high background area at Manavalakurichi - The changing trends
entry.dc:creator: Paul A.
entry.dc:description: Large-scale surface mining and refilling of the mined areas with monazite-free tailings have reduced the external radiation fields by an order of magnitude, at some locations at the natural high background areas situated in the coastal regions of peninsular India. Significant reduction by a factor of 3 has been observed in the airborne activity due to lower emanation of thoron (220Rn) at the refilled areas. The thathched huts in the area are giving way to brick and concrete structures, thus radically altering the indoor exposures. The exposure due to gamma radiation from the external surroundings was reduced by a factor of 4 due to the shielding by the construction materials. 220 Rn levels as high as 420 Bq m<sup>-3</sup> have been observed in some of the mud houses. Significant levels of 232 Th and 228 Ra were found in the urine samples collected from the adult residing in a village, situated in the high background area. © 1994.

entry.dc:title: A review of computer-based truck dispatching strategies for surface mining operations
entry.dc:creator: Munirathinarn M.
entry.prism:publicationName: International Journal of Surface Mining Reclamation and Environment
entry.dc:description: Computer-based truck dispatching systems are becoming a widely used means for improving equipment utilization and productivity at surface mining operations and for helping to insure that extraction operations at these mines meet additional performance requirements such as maintenance of stripping ratios and ore grade standards. This paper classifies existing truck dispatching strategies and examines their underlying mathematical formulations in detail. Strengths and weaknesses of the alternative approaches are identified and information on their expected performance in the field is summarized. © 1994, Taylor & Francis Group, LLC. All rights reserved.

entry.dc:title: Arch of Illinois - look to the future
entry.dc:creator: Bierei G.
entry.dc:description: The application of a more appropriate technology puts Arch of Illinois at the region's most profitable position as the mining complex undergoes a gradual shift from surface mining to underground mining. In response to dwindling low ratio reserves and increasing land acquisition and environmental costs, the mining complex shifted its attention to underground reserves. This entailed a corresponding change from truck haulage to beltline haulage. The underground operations brought about an increase in the amount of coal fines and this involved the construction of a fine coal circuit that would recover particles down to -150 μm (-100 mesh). Meanwhile, to maintain the profitability of remaining surface reserves, Arch of Illinois uses modified continuous miners and a battery haulage.

entry.dc:title: System development woes
entry.dc:creator: Neumann P.
entry.dc:description: Complex computer systems are rarely developed on time, within budget, and up to spec. In the paper are just a few examples from the RISKS archives. Among the case study presented are: Virginia system for distributing child support checks, Bank of America computerized trust accounting and reporting system, Allstate Insurance computerized automation system, Blue Cross and Blue Shield of Wisconsin with an Electronic Data System (EDS) that did not worked. Other systems discussed are the one used for the U.S. Office of surface Mining to prevent violators of strip-mine laws from getting new permits, and the Airborne Self-Protection Jammer (ASJP), an electronic air-defense system installed in over 2,00 Navy fighters and attack planes.

entry.dc:title: Speedy backfilling for old mines
entry.dc:creator: Dyni R.
entry.dc:description: There are 100,000 underground coal mines in the United States, but only 10,000 are currently in use. Many of the mines not in use are old and abandoned and are susceptible to mine subsidence. Many of these mines, accordingly, are dangerous. This article describes the filling of one such mine in Vandling, Pennsylvania. The Hillside Coal and Iron Slope was filled with two new pneumatic devices known as the high-efficiency ejector and the pneumatic pipe feeder. Sponsored by the Office of Surface Mining (OSM), the backfilling of the mine was very efficient: the mine was filled at an average rate of 122 tons/day. The high velocity of the pneumatic devices provided excellent compaction and increased density of the fill.

entry.dc:title: On-highway truck engine tackles mining applications
entry.dc:creator: Wadman B.
entry.dc:description: While engine emissions are a concern in virtually all equipment markets these days, nowhere are they more critical than in mining applications. Facing these constraints, manufacturers of mining equipment have been particularly interested in the continuing development of electronically controlled diesel engines. In dealing with the emissions question, the Wagner Mining and Construction Equipment Co. of Portland, OR, has turned to an on-highway truck engine, the electronically controlled Detroit Diesel series 60 diesel. Wagner is using the engine in both its underground and surface mining equipment and is among the first manufacturers to use the series 60 engine in a non-road application other than marine. The electronic control and diagnostic capabilities of the series 60 engine provide improved reliability in hostile underground environments. In addition, the electronic control system keeps the engine in tune without the frequent adjustments needed with mechanical control systems.

entry.dc:title: Surface-mine permitting. Who calls the shots?
entry.dc:creator: Aston R.
entry.dc:description: Until quarry and surface-mine permitting is placed solely under the control of state mining agencies and removed from local control, surface mining operators will continue to have limits set on their property rights by local authorities. Several formerly reviewed cases, as well as a 1992 New Jersey Supreme Court decision, illustrate the point. A Washington state court supported state regulation of quarries, but, in spite of this ruling, Washington county governments still exercise limited authority over quarrying that severely controls or hampers mining. In the New Jersey case, the court gave full support to local authorities in Bernardsville Borough over mining control, licensing and quarry regulation and refused to question the local community's right to impose an ordinance limiting the depth below which mining could be carried out, in order to prevent pollution of subsurface aquifers which served as a source of local drinking water.

entry.dc:title: How software can sharpen up cost estimation
entry.dc:creator: Stebbins S.
entry.dc:description: Programming the engineering processes commonly used to estimate costs can produce final-feasibility detail at pre-feasibility stages. One such package, the Western Mine Engineering's Sherpa software, is described. Sherpa is a menu driven software package designed to determine capital and operating costs for surface mining operations. Application to a shovel/truck operation stripping 35,000 t of overburden and mining 25,000 t a day is described.

entry.dc:title: Logging success of water management
entry.dc:creator: Anon
entry.dc:description: In the UK it is becoming increasingly difficult to gain approval for new sites from Public Inquiries as environmental concerns have increased. But advanced monitoring technology could help quantify the real impact of surface mining.
